label: SPF vs DKIM vs DMARC, and what each one actually checks

mentor.diagnosis: You treated the three as interchangeable anti-spoofing records. They check different things, and the one that enforces a policy is not the one that does either check.
contrast: Is the sending IP authorised to send for this domain
The From header the user actually sees; breaks on forwarding
A DNS TXT record listing permitted senders
Was the message signed by the domain and unmodified in transit
Whether the signing domain matches the visible From
A public key in DNS, signature in the header
Does SPF or DKIM pass AND align with the visible From domain, then what to do about it
Nothing new: it has no check of its own
A DNS TXT policy: none, quarantine or reject, plus reporting
mentor.rule: SPF checks the envelope sender's IP, DKIM checks the signature, DMARC checks that one of them aligns with the From address the human reads, and is the only one that can tell the receiver to reject.
mentor.tell: A stem about spoofed messages that appear to come from your own domain, or about which record to publish to stop it.
mentor.trap: SPF and DKIM both pass happily for a message whose visible From is forged, because neither looks at that header. Alignment is the gap, and DMARC exists solely to close it. Publishing SPF alone and expecting spoofing to stop is the classic mistake.

label: How web filtering is delivered and what it decides on

mentor.diagnosis: You mixed up where the filter runs with what it decides on. Delivery and decision are separate axes, and the exam asks about one or the other.
contrast: Follows the laptop off the corporate network
Needs an agent on every device; can be removed
One enforcement point, full logging, no agent
Only protects traffic routed through it
Trivial to deploy, blocks before connection
Per-domain only, bypassed by hardcoded resolvers or direct IP
Inspects the specific address, not just the host
Needs to see the URL, so TLS inspection or an agent
Broad policy by category, such as gambling or webmail
Miscategorised and brand new sites slip through
Blocks newly registered or known-bad hosts with no category yet
Scores are probabilistic, so false positives happen
Explicit allow or deny for named destinations
Manual, and does not scale alone
mentor.rule: Agent, proxy and DNS are where it runs. URL, category, reputation and explicit rules are what it decides on. A stem about remote laptops is asking about delivery; a stem about brand new malicious domains is asking about reputation.
mentor.tell: Mentions of staff working from home, or of a site too new to be categorised.
mentor.trap: DNS filtering is cheap and popular and only sees the domain. It cannot distinguish one path on a site from another, so it cannot block a single abused page on an otherwise needed service.

label: Signature-based vs trend and anomaly-based detection

mentor.diagnosis: You judged by how advanced the option sounded. The real split is whether the system is comparing against something known or against what is normal here.
contrast: Known attacks, precisely, with low false positives
Anything novel, and anything slightly altered
A learned baseline of normal behaviour
Novel and zero-day activity, insider misuse
Higher false positives, and needs a clean baseline to learn from
mentor.rule: Signatures know what bad looks like. Trend analysis knows what normal looks like. If the stem says the attack was previously unseen, no signature could have matched it.
mentor.tell: Phrases such as 'not previously seen', 'no signature exists', 'deviation from baseline', or complaints about false positive volume.
mentor.trap: Baselines learn from whatever is happening while they learn. If the environment was already compromised during baselining, the malicious behaviour becomes the definition of normal.

label: Group Policy vs SELinux: two different kinds of enforcement

mentor.diagnosis: You read them as the Windows and Linux versions of the same thing. One distributes configuration centrally; the other enforces mandatory access control inside a single kernel.
contrast: Pushes configuration and security settings to domain members
Enforces mandatory access control between processes and resources by label
Local to the host, though policy can be distributed
Mandatory: even root is bound by policy
Enforce a baseline across many machines at once
Contain a compromised service so it cannot touch what it does not need
mentor.rule: Group Policy is how you make a thousand Windows machines agree. SELinux is how you stop one Linux process doing something its label does not permit, including when it is running as root.
mentor.tell: A stem about rolling a setting out across a domain, versus one about confining a service that has been exploited.
mentor.trap: SELinux constraining root is the part people disbelieve. It is the whole point of mandatory access control: the policy sits above the account, not under it.

label: File integrity monitoring vs DLP vs user behaviour analytics

mentor.diagnosis: You chose the capability with the most familiar name rather than the one watching the thing in the question. Each watches a different noun: files, data leaving, or people.
contrast: Data in motion, in use and at rest, by content
Sensitive content is sent, copied or uploaded against policy
Care who the user is, beyond policy scope
Patterns of account activity against a baseline
An account behaves unlike itself or unlike its peers
Process, file and network activity on the endpoint
Malicious execution or persistence is observed
Devices joining the network and their posture
An unknown or non-compliant device connects
mentor.rule: FIM watches files, DLP watches data leaving, UBA watches people, EDR watches processes, NAC watches the door.
mentor.tell: A stem naming what is being protected or observed: a configuration file, a spreadsheet of customer records, or an account suddenly behaving oddly.
mentor.trap: A departing employee emailing customer data out is a DLP question. The same employee signing in at 03:00 from a new country is a UBA question. The scenario often contains both, so read what the control is being asked to catch.

label: ACL rule order and first match wins

mentor.diagnosis: You wrote rules that are individually correct but in an order that makes some of them unreachable. An ACL is evaluated top to bottom and stops at the first match.
contrast: Below a broad rule that already matched
Placed before the permit for its subnet
Placed after, so it never runs
mentor.rule: Specific before general, always. If a broader rule above already matches the traffic, everything below it for that traffic is dead code.
mentor.tell: Any task mixing a subnet wide permit with a single host deny is testing ordering. Put the exception first.
mentor.trap: The rule set looks complete because every required line is present. Graders simulate the traffic, so a shadowed rule scores as if you never wrote it.

label: The implicit deny at the end of an ACL

mentor.diagnosis: You either added an explicit permit any at the end, or you assumed traffic not mentioned would be allowed. Firewalls deny by default.
contrast: Yes, at the bottom of every ACL
Yes, which is why you add it
Adding permit any at the end
mentor.rule: Anything you did not explicitly permit is already denied. Write an explicit deny any at the bottom only to get logging, never a permit any.
mentor.tell: 'Deny all other traffic' in the requirements usually needs no rule at all. It is already true. Check whether the task wants it logged.
mentor.trap: 'Deny all other traffic' reads like an instruction to add a rule, and adding an explicit deny any is harmless. Adding permit any is the failure, and it is the option that makes the other requirements appear to pass.

label: Source vs destination, and which side holds the well known port

mentor.diagnosis: You put the service port on the wrong side of the rule, or reversed source and destination. The server listens on the well known port, the client uses a random high port.
contrast: Your host, on an ephemeral port
mentor.rule: The destination port is the service. The source port is almost always any. Write the rule in the direction the connection is initiated.
mentor.tell: 'Allow the internet to reach the web server' means destination is the server and destination port is 443. Never source port 443.
mentor.trap: Source port 443 looks symmetric and tidy. It matches only the return traffic, which a stateful firewall already handles.

label: Using any where the requirement named a specific host or port

mentor.diagnosis: Your rule permits the required traffic, but also a great deal more. Passing the functional test is not the same as passing least privilege.
contrast: Exactly the host, port and direction required
any, or a whole subnet, or all ports
Partial credit at best, often zero for that subtask
mentor.rule: Use any only where the requirement genuinely says any, which is usually only the source of inbound internet traffic.
mentor.tell: If the scenario names a specific management workstation, the source must be that host's address, not its subnet and not any.
mentor.trap: The traffic test passes, so the rule feels correct. Graders check breadth as well as function, exactly as a real auditor would.

label: EDR and XDR vs traditional antivirus

mentor.diagnosis: You reached for signature based antivirus against something with no signature.
contrast: Yes, across endpoint, network, mail and cloud
Isolate the host, kill the process, roll back
mentor.rule: No signature yet means behaviour based detection, which means EDR. XDR is EDR correlated beyond the endpoint.
mentor.tell: 'Zero day', 'fileless', 'living off the land', or 'we need to see what the process did before it was caught' all point to EDR.
mentor.trap: Updating antivirus definitions is a real and sensible action, which makes it a convincing distractor against a threat that has no definition to update.
